t: Aim and plan of the session
n: This laboratory session is devoted to detecting barium and lead in the mineralisate. The plan has two parts: first, detection of the barium cation in the mineralisate; second, detection of the lead cation in the mineralisate. The aim is to introduce the toxicological significance and methods of analysis of certain metallic poisons isolated by mineralisation with sulphuric and nitric acids. Students master the conditions for analysing substances containing barium and lead in pure solutions and in a solution of unknown composition.

Four outcomes are expected from the session. First, isolating the precipitate from the mineralisate. Second, separating the barium and lead sulphates in the precipitate from each other. Third, establishing the identity of the barium and lead cations. Fourth, identifying the unknown substance given by the instructor and summarising the result in the laboratory notebook; the conclusion is confirmed and signed by the group instructor.

The apparatus and equipment needed for the work: mineralisate, filter paper, funnel, reagents, test tubes, demonstration materials, adhesive tape and paper. For the barium analysis a microscope slide, platinum wire and a microscope are needed; the reagents are concentrated H2SO4, 10% HCl, 10% potassium iodate, potassium chromate or dichromate and sodium rhodizonate. In the lead analysis, dithizone, 0.01% in chloroform, hydroxylamine hydrochloride 10%, ammonia 10%, chloroform, 1N HNO3 and NaOH, and universal indicator are used.

We turn to the LD50 values of metallic poisons. For arsenic and antimony compounds LD50 = 0.08-0.1 g, for thallium 0.5 g, for chromium 0.2-1 g, for cadmium 0.03 g, for mercury 0.2-0.3 g. For ZnCl2 LD50 = 5.0 g, for KMnO4 15-20 g. Compounds of chromium and manganese in the higher valency state have a stronger effect. Organic compounds of mercury have a strong toxic effect.

General signs of metal poisoning. In poisoning with salts of heavy metals and arsenic, thirst, vomiting, diarrhoea, stomach pain and bleeding from the internal organs are observed. The vomit is characteristic of the metal: green with chromium and copper, brown with manganese; the victim perceives a metallic taste in the mouth. With lead, black spots appear on the gums, and with bismuth and mercury, white spots. With cadmium, internal bleeding is observed, and with copper, nosebleed.

t: Objects for examination for metallic poisons
n: Because metal-containing substances form part of the body's trace elements and enzymes, determining the quantity of the toxic cation is an essential requirement. Arsenic, lead and mercury have the property of accumulating in the body; in poisoning with arsenic and mercury death occurs in 50% of cases. Metals cause fat to accumulate in parenchymal organs. Objects for examination: stomach, small and large intestine, liver and gallbladder, kidney, and also urine, vomit, hair, nails and bones.

The uses of barium compounds. Barium carbonate is used mixed with flour to exterminate mice and rats; children may eat it. Barium chloride, nitrate and hydroxide are used as reagents, and barium chloride is used in the textile and rubber industries. Barium carbonate is used in making glass and porcelain. BaCO3 and BaSeO3 are used in agriculture against pests.

Barium poisoning. Barium compounds are toxic: 0.8-0.9 g of BaCO3 is considered a toxic dose. In poisoning, burning in the stomach and mouth, salivation, nausea, abdominal pain, vomiting and diarrhoea are observed. The rhythm of the heartbeat is disturbed and blood pressure rises. The heart muscles fail, and death occurs with consciousness retained: paralysis of the heart.

The procedure for isolating the precipitate. If there is a precipitate in the mineralisate, it is filtered off and the filtrate is transferred to a 200 ml volumetric flask. The precipitate on the filter is washed with 10 ml of 0.1% sulphuric acid and 10 ml of water. The washings are added to the filtrate, and the volume of the mixture is made up to 200 ml.

t: Role of the precipitate and filtrate
n: The role of the precipitate and the filtrate. The precipitate is tested for barium and lead, and the filtrate for zinc and other cations. The colour of the precipitate depends on its composition. A white precipitate consists of Ba, Pb and Ca sulphates. In a dirty bluish precipitate, the cations Cr, Cu, Fe and Al are precipitated together.

Separating barium and lead sulphates. The precipitate is washed dropwise with 5-10 ml of hot ammonium acetate solution with excess acetic acid. Barium sulphate remains on the filter paper as an undissolved precipitate. Lead sulphate, however, dissolves in the ammonium acetate and passes into the filtrate. Thus, BaSO4 is on the filter and Pb acetate is in the filtrate.

t: Dissolution of Pb sulphate in ammonium acetate
n: Let us consider the dissolution of lead sulphate in ammonium acetate. In the denitrated mineralisate, lead sulphate may be present in the precipitate together with barium sulphate. Before the barium sulphate precipitate is examined, lead sulphate is separated from it. For this the precipitate is washed with a hot solution of ammonium acetate acidified with acetic acid. As a result PbSO4 passes into Pb(CH3COO)2 and (NH4)2SO4, and BaSO4 remains on the filter.

Detecting barium by recrystallisation of the sulphate. Part of the precipitate is transferred to a microscope slide, and 1-2 drops of concentrated sulphuric acid are applied. It is carefully heated over a low flame until white vapour forms; the process is repeated 2-3 times. After cooling for 15-20 minutes, colourless microcrystals resembling the shape (Q, x) are seen under the microscope, that is, small lens-shaped or "+"-shaped crystals. The shape is drawn in the notebook.

Barium iodate microcrystals. Part of the precipitate is transferred to platinum wire and held in the flame for a few seconds. The part of the platinum wire carrying the precipitate is dipped into 1-2 drops of 10% hydrochloric acid; the process is repeated 2-3 times. To the solution on the microscope slide, 1-2 drops of 10% potassium iodate are added. After a few minutes, rod-shaped microcrystals of barium iodate, that is, Ba(IO3)2, are seen.

t: Barium analysis: flame and chemical changes
n: Flame and chemical changes in barium analysis. If a BaSO4 precipitate is heated on platinum wire in a gas flame, the flame is coloured green and the precipitate is partially reduced to BaS: BaSO4 + 4CO → BaS + 4CO2. BaS is converted into BaCl2 by hydrochloric acid. If Na2SO4 is added to BaCl2, BaSO4 is precipitated again; if KIO3 is added, Ba(IO3)2 forms. Ba(IO3)2 forms colourless prismatic crystals spread out in spheroid form.

Precipitation reactions of barium. In the reaction with chromate and dichromate, a pale yellow precipitate of barium chromate forms; it dissolves in mineral acid and does not dissolve in acetic acid. With H2SO4 or sulphates a white precipitate forms, insoluble in mineral acid and alkali. With sodium rhodizonate a red-brown colour forms.

The quantity of barium is determined by two methods: gravimetric and volumetric. In the gravimetric method the precipitate is dissolved in an ammoniacal solution of Trilon B and filtered; the filtrate is acidified, and BaSO4 is isolated, dried and weighed. In the volumetric method the precipitate is dissolved in Trilon B solution, and the excess Trilon B is titrated with ZnCl2 using eriochrome blue indicator. In this the blue colour changes to red.

The sodium rhodizonate reaction. The barium ion gives a reddish-brown precipitate with sodium rhodizonate. Under the action of 1 drop of hydrochloric acid the precipitate turns bright red; if the colour arose from strontium, it disappears. With chromate and dichromate, barium gives a yellow precipitate that dissolves in mineral acid and does not dissolve in acetic acid.

Lead: uses and action. Lead is used in printing and in accumulators; 2PbCO3·Pb(OH)2 is a white paint, and PbSO4 is used in preparing paints. TEL, that is, tetraethyllead, is added to petrol as an antiknock agent; basic lead acetate is used in medicine. The lead ion combines with the sulphydryl groups of enzymes and proteins and disrupts the nervous system. After absorption into the blood, 90% of it binds to erythrocytes.

Detecting lead with dithizone. The examination begins with the dithizonate reaction; if it is positive, macro- and microreactions are carried out. Procedure: to 0.5 ml of Pb acetate solution, 1 ml of 10% hydroxylamine and 1 ml of 10% ammonia are added, giving a pH of 7.5. Then 5 ml of chloroform and a 0.01% solution of dithizone in chloroform are added, and the mixture is shaken for 30 seconds. If lead is present, the chloroform layer is coloured red-pink.

Dithizonate and masking. If a chloroform solution of dithizone is added to the solution obtained by dissolving the precipitate, the chloroform layer is coloured bright red. The reaction proceeds in the pH range 7-10. To mask interfering ions, KCN or hydroxylamine is added. This reaction has negative forensic chemical significance. The chloroform layer is separated and shaken with nitric acid; this is called re-extraction.

Re-extraction of the dithizonate. The chloroform layer is separated and shaken with nitric acid solution. Lead dithizonate decomposes, and the lead passes as Pb(NO3)2 into the aqueous layer, while the dithizone remains in the chloroform. The aqueous layer is separated and additionally tested for the lead ion.

Isolating and purifying lead. If the result is positive, the whole filtrate is extracted 2-3 times with dithizone and chloroform. The combined chloroform layer is shaken with 5 ml of 1N HNO3 for 1 minute; Pb passes as nitrate into the aqueous layer. The aqueous layer is brought to pH 5 with 1N NaOH, divided into five portions, and qualitative reactions are carried out.

Precipitation reactions of lead. The reactions of lead with sulphide, sulphate and chromate are carried out on a microscope slide. With hydrogen sulphide water, that is, H2S, a black precipitate forms. With 10% sulphuric acid a white precipitate or turbidity appears. With 10% K chromate or dichromate a yellow precipitate forms, which dissolves in alkali. For each reaction an equation is written and an explanation is given according to forensic chemical requirements.

There are three methods of quantifying lead. The first is the PEC method: the quantity of lead is determined from the coloured solution formed with dithizone. The second is complexometric, that is, the volumetric trilonometric method, in which the indicator is eriochrome black. The third is the dichromate-iodometric method: it is based on forming lead chromate followed by an iodometric finish.

There are two microcrystalloscopic reactions of lead. The first is the hexanitrite: 3-4 drops of solution are evaporated on the slide, and copper acetate and potassium nitrite are applied to the residue; brown square-shaped crystals are seen under the microscope. The second is caesium chloride and KI: 4-5 drops of solution are evaporated to dryness, and 2-3 drops of 30% acetic acid are applied to the residue, with a crystal of CsCl on one side and a crystal of KI on the opposite side. If lead is present, yellow-green needle-shaped crystals form in the second reaction. The shape of the crystals is drawn in the notebook.

The hexanitrite reaction of lead. To 1 drop of the isolated solution on a microscope slide, 1-2 drops of 1% copper acetate are added and the mixture is evaporated to dryness. To the residue, 2-3 drops of 30% acetic acid and a crystal of potassium nitrite are added. As a result, black-brown microcrystals of four-cornered cubic shape form. Their composition is K2Cu[Pb(NO2)6].

t: Lead: caesium chloride and KI reaction
n: The reaction of lead with caesium chloride and KI. On a microscope slide, 4-5 drops of aqueous solution are evaporated, and then 2-3 drops of 30% acetic acid and crystals of CsCl and KI are added. Yellow-green needle-shaped crystals of Cs[PbI3] form. The crystal shape is drawn in the notebook.

Tetraethyllead, TEL for short, is an antiknock agent: an organometallic compound added to fuel to prevent failure of internal combustion engines. TEL is a colourless liquid with a foul odour, insoluble in water and readily soluble in petrol; it boils at 198-200 °C with decomposition. On burning it forms a long, thin flame and yellowish-white smoke. The smoke is toxic because it consists of PbO particles.

Isolating TEL from the object. From the organs of a corpse and from foodstuffs, TEL is isolated by steam distillation; the distillate is collected in a saturated alcoholic solution of iodine. From plant objects, that is, flour, bread and cereals, the material is steeped in chloroform for 2 hours and iodine is added to the filtrate. For petrol and kerosene, 20 ml of petrol is mixed with 20 ml of 4% alcoholic iodine solution and evaporated after 30 minutes. The residue is tested for Pb2+.

The "Wheel" training. The table includes 7 reactions: dithizone, caesium chloride + KI, sulphuric acid, hydrogen sulphide, copper acetate + potassium nitrite, potassium chromate and sodium rhodizonate. Each reaction is completed in the barium and lead columns. Task: correctly choose the colour reactions characteristic of barium and lead cations, and show the chemistry of the reactions.

t: Case 9: death after an X-ray examination
n: Case 9: death after an X-ray examination. A person, "X", underwent an X-ray examination, came home, his health deteriorated, and he died by the evening. He was sent for forensic chemical examination together with the contents of his stomach. Task: to explain the incident, determine for which substance the analysis is to be carried out, and carry out the forensic chemical analysis. A barium compound used as a medicine is indicated as a possible cause, and the analysis is carried out in the precipitate for Ba and Pb.

Situational problem. Portions of the internal organs of the corpse of Sh. Aliyev, born in 2000, were brought to the city forensic medical department in separate sealed 500 g glass jars. Physical evidence: liver 100 g, kidneys 250 g, portions of stomach and intestine 300 g. According to the investigation, he had been inhaling petrol and shoe polish fumes; he was given a barium sulphate suspension to drink for an X-ray, and died from an adverse effect. Forensic chemical examination: analysis is to be carried out for the metals lead and barium.

The first part of the review questions. First: what reaction is used to separate lead and barium cations from each other? Second: what chemical reactions are used in detecting lead in toxicological examination? Third: name the methods of quantifying the lead cation. Fourth: name the methods of isolating tetraethyllead from various objects and determining it qualitatively and quantitatively.

The second part of the review questions. First: by what method is the barium cation converted from the barium sulphate precipitate into a soluble state? Second: on what reactions is the qualitative detection of the barium cation based? Third: what chemical significance do the reactions forming barium sulphate and barium iodate have? Fourth: which methods are used in toxicological chemistry analyses to quantify the barium ion?

Safety and working procedure. In recrystallising barium sulphate, concentrated sulphuric acid is added dropwise and heated carefully over a low flame. In detecting lead, one works with chloroform and dithizone solution, 1N nitric acid and sodium hydroxide. The student who has finished the work has the correctness of the results checked by the instructor.

t: Ba and Pb: general sequence of detection
n: We summarise the general sequence for detecting barium and lead. A precipitate is separated from the mineralisate: the precipitate is tested for barium and lead, and the filtrate for zinc and other cations. With hot ammonium acetate, BaSO4 remains on the filter and Pb passes into the filtrate. Barium is confirmed by several reactions, and lead starting from the dithizone reaction.

t: Microcrystals to be drawn in the notebook
n: Microcrystals drawn in the notebook. Barium sulphate: colourless microcrystals resembling the shape (Q, x); the reaction equation is written and the shape is drawn in the notebook. Barium iodate: rod-shaped microcrystals; the equations are written and the shape is drawn. For lead, the brown square crystals of the hexanitrite and the yellow-green needle-shaped crystals with caesium chloride + KI are drawn.

Recording and assessing the result. The unknown substances given by the instructor are isolated and identified. The correctness of the identified substance is checked by the instructor against the physical evidence. The results are summarised in the practical work notebook, a conclusion is written, and the group instructor confirms it with a signature.
